name: Musubi dachi
description: Heels together, toes turned out about 45°, arms relaxed at the sides. This is where you stand to bow in and out of the dojo.

name: Heikō dachi
description: Feet parallel and about shoulder-width apart, weight even, knees soft. The natural standing position most kata open from.

name: Sanchin dachi
description: Gōjū-ryū's signature stance. One foot half a step forward, both feet turned in, knees drawn together and the whole body under tension while you breathe.

name: Neko ashi dachi
description: Roughly 90% of the weight sits on the bent back leg. Only the ball of the front foot rests on the floor, so it can kick or slide without a weight shift.

name: Shiko dachi
description: A wide, deep stance with the feet turned out 45° and the knees pressed open over them. Hips sink straight down — it builds rooting and hip power.

name: Zenkutsu dachi
description: Long stance with about 70% of the weight on the bent front leg and the back leg driven straight. Used to deliver stepping techniques forward.

name: Kōkutsu dachi
description: The mirror of front stance: weight loads onto the bent rear leg, front leg light and straight. A defensive stance that lets you pull back out of range.

name: Tsuru ashi dachi
description: Balanced on one bent leg with the other foot tucked in behind the supporting knee. Appears in Seiyunchin and Kururunfa, usually just before a kick or a drop.

name: Choku zuki
description: The basic punch: fist travels straight out from the hip, forearm rotating so the knuckles land palm-down. No step — practised on the spot from a natural stance.

name: Oi zuki
description: Step forward into front stance and punch with the hand on the same side as the leading leg, so the whole body mass travels behind the fist.

name: Gyaku zuki
description: From front stance, the rear hand punches as the hips snap square to the target. Karate's main power punch — the hip rotation, not the arm, supplies the force.

name: Kizami zuki
description: A fast snapping punch with the lead hand from fighting stance. Used to measure distance, interrupt an attack, or open the way for something heavier.

name: Mawashi zuki
description: A hooking punch that swings in a horizontal arc with the elbow lifted, landing on the side of the jaw or ribs rather than straight on.

name: Ura zuki
description: A short punch thrown with the elbow still bent, palm facing up. Made for infighting range, where a full extension would overshoot the target.

name: Uraken uchi
description: The arm folds across the chest, then the fist whips out from the elbow and snaps back, landing with the back of the knuckles on the temple or ribs.

name: Shutō uchi
description: An open-hand chop with the outer edge of the palm, swung in from beside the ear into the neck or collarbone. The hand stays firm with the thumb tucked.

name: Haitō uchi
description: The mirror of the knife-hand: the strike sweeps outward and lands on the thumb-side edge of the hand, typically into the neck or the side of the head.

name: Tettsui uchi
description: The bottom of the clenched fist drops like a hammer — straight down onto a collarbone or grabbing arm, or sideways into the ribs. Heavy rather than fast.

name: Empi uchi
description: At close range the elbow becomes the weapon, driven forward, up, back or across. Short travel, very little that can go wrong, and nothing to break.

name: Nukite
description: Fingers held straight and braced together, thrust like a blade into soft targets — the throat, the floating ribs, the solar plexus.

name: Mae geri
description: The knee lifts first, then the lower leg snaps straight out and back again. Contact is with the ball of the foot, toes pulled back out of the way.

name: Mawashi geri
description: The knee comes up to the side, then the hip rotates over and the leg whips around parallel to the floor. Lands with the instep, ball of the foot, or shin.

name: Yoko geri
description: The kick travels sideways with the body leaning away from it, striking with the outer edge of the foot (sokutō) rather than the ball.

name: Ushiro geri
description: A kick driven straight out behind you, heel first, with the body folding forward as the leg extends. Usually thrown after turning.

name: Hiza geri
description: The knee is driven upward into the body at close range, normally while both hands pull the opponent down onto it.

name: Kansetsu geri
description: A low stamping kick into the side or front of the knee joint. Short, blunt and aimed at taking the opponent's base away.

name: Kin geri
description: A rising snap kick to the groin using the instep or shin. Short travel, no wind-up, often thrown off the back leg in kihon combinations.

name: Age uke
description: The forearm travels up and outward to lift a head-height attack clear, finishing at an angle just above the forehead with the fist past the far temple.

name: Gedan barai
description: The arm sweeps down and across the front of the body to clear a low attack such as a front kick, finishing above the leading thigh.

name: Soto uke
description: The forearm comes from outside the body inward across the centreline, catching a chest-height punch on the outer edge of the arm.

name: Uchi uke
description: The opposite path to soto uke — the forearm starts near the body and drives outward, pushing the attack away from the centreline.

name: Shutō uke
description: An open-hand guard: the leading hand blocks with the palm edge while the other stays at the solar plexus. Almost always paired with back stance.

name: Mawashi uke
description: Gōjū-ryū's own two-handed block, drawn from Sanchin and Tenshō. Both open hands turn through a circle — one high, one low — redirecting rather than meeting force.

name: Kake uke
description: The hand hooks over the incoming arm and pulls it off line, trapping the attacker for a moment so the other hand can strike into the gap.

name: Rei
description: The bow. Used entering and leaving the dojo, and to the sensei and partners. Eyes stay up in a martial context.

name: Ritsurei
description: Bow performed from standing, normally from musubi dachi.

name: Zarei
description: Bow performed from seiza, hands placed left then right on the floor.

name: Seiza
description: Kneeling posture used at the start and end of class, usually with mokusō.

name: Mokusō
description: A short period of stillness and breathing to settle the mind before or after training.

name: Kiotsuke
description: Command to come to attention.

name: Yōi
description: Command to assume the ready position, normally heikō dachi.

name: Hajime
description: Command to start.

name: Yame
description: Command to stop.

name: Mawatte
description: Command to turn and face the other way, used in moving basics.

name: Naore
description: Command to return to the natural position.

name: Sensei
description: The instructor. Literally one who has gone before.

name: Sempai
description: A student senior to you in the dojo.

name: Dōjō
description: The place of the way — where training happens.

name: Dōgi
description: The uniform, commonly shortened to gi. Gōjū-ryū gi are traditionally heavier and shorter in the sleeve.

name: Obi
description: The belt, showing grade. Tied with the knot centred and both ends level.

name: Jōdan
description: Head and neck height. A technique named jōdan is aimed there.

name: Chūdan
description: Chest and stomach height — the most common target level in kihon.

name: Gedan
description: Below the belt: groin, thighs, knees.

name: Hidari
description: Left side. Hidari sanchin dachi means left foot forward.

name: Migi
description: Right side.

name: Mae
description: Forward. As in mae geri, front kick.

name: Ushiro
description: Behind. As in ushiro geri, back kick.

name: Yoko
description: Sideways. As in yoko geri, side kick.

name: Soto
description: From outside inward, describing the path of a block or strike.

name: Uchi
description: From inside outward. Also means strike when used as uchi waza.

name: Gyaku
description: Opposite side to the leading leg, as in gyaku zuki.

name: Morote
description: Two-handed version of a technique, as in morote uke.

name: Seiken
description: The first two knuckles of a closed fist — the standard punching surface.

name: Uraken
description: The back of the knuckles, used in whipping strikes.

name: Tettsui
description: The muscled bottom edge of the fist.

name: Shutō
description: The outer edge of the open hand, thumb tucked.

name: Haitō
description: The thumb-side edge of the open hand.

name: Teishō
description: The heel of the palm — a favourite Gōjū-ryū striking surface.

name: Nukite
description: Braced fingertips used against soft targets.

name: Hiji / Empi
description: The elbow, used at close range.

name: Hiza
description: The knee, used in clinch range.

name: Koshi
description: The ball of the foot, with toes pulled back. Used in mae geri.

name: Sokutō
description: The outer blade of the foot, used in yoko geri.

name: Kakato
description: The heel, used in stamping and back kicks.

name: Gō
description: The hard half of the style's name: linear, direct, forceful technique.

name: Jū
description: The soft half of the name: yielding, circular, redirecting technique. Gōjū means hard-soft.

name: Kihon
description: The fundamental techniques, practised on the spot or moving (ido kihon).

name: Kata
description: A fixed sequence of techniques that stores the system's knowledge.

name: Bunkai
description: Taking a kata apart to work out what the movements are actually for.

name: Kumite
description: Partner work, from fixed pre-arranged drills through to free sparring.

name: Kiai
description: The shout at the moment of commitment, tightening the abdomen and focusing the technique.

name: Kime
description: The instant of total tension at the end of a technique, then immediate release.

name: Zanshin
description: Continued awareness after a technique finishes — you have not switched off.

name: Muchimi
description: A heavy, adhering quality of movement particular to Gōjū-ryū, felt in kake uke and mawashi uke.

name: Chinkuchi
description: An Okinawan term for locking the whole body for an instant at the point of impact.

name: Hōjō undō
description: Conditioning with traditional tools — chiishi, nigiri game, ishi sashi, makiwara.

name: Tanden
description: The point below the navel treated as the body's centre of power and breathing.

name: Ibuki
description: The audible tensioned breathing used in Sanchin.

name: Ido
description: Moving basics — technique performed while stepping, as opposed to on the spot.

name: Tai sabaki
description: Moving the body off the line of attack rather than meeting it head on.

name: Sanchin
description: The core kata of the style: slow, tensed, breathing-driven. Everything else is built on it.

name: Tenshō
description: The soft counterpart to Sanchin, using open-hand circular movement.

name: Gekisai dai ichi
description: The first kata taught, developed by Chōjun Miyagi in the 1940s to introduce basics.

name: Gekisai dai ni
description: Follows Gekisai dai ichi and introduces open-hand technique, neko ashi dachi and muchimi.

name: Saifa
description: Introduces body evasion, hammer fists and rapid changes of direction.

name: Seiyunchin
description: Contains no kicks. Built on shiko dachi and pulling, off-balancing hand work.

name: Shisōchin
description: Open-hand thrusts and elbow techniques worked in four directions.

name: Sanseru
description: Attacks the limbs and joints, with low kicks and close-range entries.

name: Sēpai
description: Advanced kata mixing circular deflection with sudden angular attack.

name: Kururunfa
english: holding on long and striking suddenly
description: Marked by long pauses then explosive bursts, with heavy use of neko ashi dachi.

name: Sēsan
description: Direct, linear kata focused on close-range control and precise angles.

name: Suparinpei
description: The longest and most advanced kata in the system, containing the whole curriculum.
